content: Web accessibility refers to the practice of designing and developing websites in a way that ensures they are usable by individuals of all abilities and disabilities. Properly designed websites allow all users to have equal access to information and functionality. For instance, when a website is coded using semantically meaningful HTML, includes textual equivalents for images, and provides descriptive link names, it becomes accessible to blind users who rely on text-to-speech software or text-to-Braille hardware. Similarly, when text and images are large or can be enlarged, users with visual impairments can more easily read and comprehend the content. When links are both underlined and color-coded, colorblind users can still identify them. Large clickable areas and links benefit users who have difficulty controlling a mouse with precision, such as those with motor impairments. Websites that allow navigation using only a keyboard or a single-switch access device accommodate users who cannot use a mouse or a standard keyboard. Closed captions or sign language versions of videos enable deaf and hard-of-hearing users to understand video content. Avoiding or providing options to disable flashing effects reduces the risk of seizures for users prone to photosensitive epilepsy. Writing content in plain language and supplementing it with instructional diagrams and animations helps users with dyslexia or learning difficulties better understand the material. When websites are built and maintained correctly, they can accommodate all users, including those with disabilities, without negatively affecting usability for non-disabled users. Disabilities that may require such accommodations include motor impairments (e.g., Parkinson's disease, muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, or stroke), auditory impairments (e.g., deafness or hearing loss), seizure disorders (e.g., photosensitive epilepsy), and cognitive or intellectual disabilities (e.g., developmental disabilities, dyslexia, or dyscalculia). Assistive technologies play a crucial role in enabling web browsing for individuals with disabilities. These include: Screen reader software, which uses synthesized speech to read selected elements or all on-screen activity, aiding users with visual impairments or learning difficulties. Braille terminals, which render text as Braille characters using a refreshable Braille display and may include a QWERTY or Braille keyboard. Screen magnification software, which enlarges on-screen content for users with vision impairments. Speech recognition software, which allows users to control the computer with spoken commands or convert dictation into grammatically correct text, benefiting those who struggle with using a mouse or keyboard. Keyboard overlays, which make typing easier and more accurate for users with motor control difficulties. Globally, web accessibility guidelines have been widely adopted to create accessible websites. For example, the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) have been updated over the years to remain relevant and technology-neutral. However, these guidelines have faced criticism for being difficult to navigate and understand. In the Philippines, the government has taken steps to promote web accessibility through initiatives like the Biwako Millennium Framework and the Manila Accessible ICT Design Recommendations. Spain has implemented UNE 139803 to regulate web accessibility, while Sweden integrates accessibility into the entire lifecycle of public sector websites through its national guidelines. The UK has published PAS 78, which outlines best practices for commissioning accessible websites, and the Disability Discrimination Act (DDA) prohibits discrimination against people with disabilities, including in web services. In Australia, a landmark court case in 2000 established the legal requirement for accessible websites under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992. Ireland's Disability Act 2005 is supported by a Code of Practice to ensure compliance with accessibility standards. Website accessibility audits are increasingly common and involve identifying and addressing accessibility issues. Methods include: Automated tools, which quickly process many pages but may miss certain issues. Expert technical reviews, which provide detailed feedback but are time-consuming and may not cover large websites comprehensively. User testing, which identifies usability and accessibility problems but must be conducted carefully to avoid over-reliance on individual user preferences. Ideally, a combination of these methods should be used to thoroughly assess a website's accessibility.
